units.title: The Baroque
units.blurb: Drama, motion and light: Caravaggio and Bernini in Rome, Velázquez in Spain, Rubens and Van Dyck in Flanders, and Baroque building.

units.title: The Dutch Golden Age
units.blurb: Rembrandt, Vermeer, Judith Leyster, and the landscapes and still lifes made for a market of buyers.

units.title: The Eighteenth Century
units.blurb: Rococo grace, the Grand Manner portrait, Neoclassicism, and art in colonial and early America.

units.title: Romanticism and Realism
units.blurb: Feeling and the sublime, the Hudson River School, Realism, photography and American painting after the Civil War.

units.title: Asia and the Islamic World, 1500 to 1900
units.blurb: Ukiyo-e woodblock prints, Japanese screens, Ming and Qing China, Joseon Korea, the Mughal, Ottoman and Safavid empires.

units.title: Impressionism and After
units.blurb: Painting light and modern life, Monet's series, Seurat, Van Gogh, Cézanne, Gauguin, and the pull of Japanese prints.

units.title: African and Native American Arts
units.blurb: Masks, figures and textiles in Africa, the Benin Bronzes, and the arts of Native North America.

units.title: Modern Art to Mid-Century
units.blurb: Fauvism, Expressionism, Cubism, Futurism, Dada, De Stijl and the Bauhaus, Surrealism, modern architecture and photography, and Abstract Expressionism.

units.title: Recognizing Styles
units.blurb: Telling periods apart, dating a work by its style, and comparing two works.

topics.title: What Makes Art Baroque
topics.short: Baroque art (about 1600 to 1750) uses drama, motion, strong light and dark, and diagonal compositions to pull the viewer in; the Catholic Church and kings were its great patrons.
topics.trouble: People use "baroque" to mean just "fancy." The style is about drama and involving the viewer, not decoration alone.

topics.title: Caravaggio and Tenebrism
topics.short: Caravaggio painted ordinary-looking people lit by a sharp beam in deep darkness (tenebrism), as in The Calling of Saint Matthew (1599–1600).
topics.trouble: People mix up chiaroscuro and tenebrism. Chiaroscuro is any modeling with light and dark; tenebrism is its extreme, with most of the picture in deep shadow.

topics.title: Artemisia Gentileschi
topics.short: Artemisia Gentileschi, a follower of Caravaggio, was the first woman admitted to Florence's Academy of the Arts of Drawing (1616); her Self-Portrait as the Allegory of Painting shows her at work.
topics.trouble: People think there were no women artists before modern times. Gentileschi, Sofonisba Anguissola, Judith Leyster and Rachel Ruysch were famous in their day.

topics.title: Bernini and Baroque Rome
topics.short: Gian Lorenzo Bernini, sculptor and architect, shaped Rome: his colonnade (1656–1667) wraps St. Peter's Square like open arms.
topics.trouble: People think Baroque buildings are just Renaissance ones with more ornament. Baroque architects bent walls and spaces into curves that seem to move.

topics.title: Velázquez and Spain
topics.short: Diego Velázquez, court painter to Philip IV, painted Las Meninas (1656), a puzzle of looking in which the painter, the princess and a mirror all watch us.
topics.trouble: People think Las Meninas is a simple group portrait. Who is being painted, and where the viewer stands, are open questions that scholars still debate.

topics.title: Rubens and Van Dyck
topics.short: Peter Paul Rubens ran a huge Antwerp workshop and painted with energetic color; his assistant Anthony van Dyck became court painter to Charles I of England.
topics.trouble: People think a "Rubens" was painted by Rubens alone. Large works came from his workshop, with the master designing and finishing.

topics.title: Palaces and Domes
topics.short: Versailles (enlarged from the 1660s) showed royal power in a palace and gardens; Christopher Wren rebuilt St. Paul's Cathedral in London (1675–1710) after the Great Fire.
topics.trouble: People think Versailles was always a palace. It began as a royal hunting lodge that Louis XIV enlarged.

topics.title: Art for a Market: The Dutch Republic
topics.short: In the 1600s the Dutch Republic had few church commissions and many middle-class buyers, so artists painted portraits, landscapes, still lifes and scenes of daily life to sell.
topics.trouble: People think painters always worked on commission. Dutch artists often painted first and sold through dealers and fairs.

topics.title: Rembrandt
topics.short: Rembrandt van Rijn painted the group portrait The Night Watch (1642) full of motion and light, and searching self-portraits throughout his life.
topics.trouble: People think The Night Watch is a night scene. It is set in daylight; a darkened varnish made it look like night until it was cleaned.

topics.title: Vermeer and the Quiet Interior
topics.short: Johannes Vermeer of Delft painted calm rooms lit from a side window, such as The Milkmaid (about 1660; some scholars say a little earlier), using tiny dots of light and costly ultramarine.
topics.trouble: People state as fact that Vermeer traced a camera obscura image. Some scholars think he used one; others disagree, and there is no direct evidence.

topics.title: Judith Leyster and the Genre Scene
topics.short: Judith Leyster, one of the first women in Haarlem's painters' guild, painted lively genre scenes and a famous self-portrait at her easel (about 1630).
topics.trouble: People think Leyster's works were by Frans Hals. Some were sold under his name until her monogram was found in the 1890s.

topics.title: Landscape and Still Life
topics.short: Jacob van Ruisdael painted skies over flat land and windmills; still lifes of flowers, food and skulls (vanitas) by Rachel Ruysch and Pieter Claesz reminded viewers that life is short.
topics.trouble: People think a flower still life shows one real bouquet. Painters combined flowers that bloom in different seasons from separate studies.

topics.title: Rococo and the Elegant Portrait
topics.short: Rococo (about 1720 to 1780) brought light pastel color, curving ornament and elegant pleasure; Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun painted Queen Marie Antoinette.
topics.trouble: People think Rococo is a heavier Baroque. It is lighter: pastel colors, small scale, delicate curves.

topics.title: Chardin, Canaletto and the Grand Tour
topics.short: Jean-Siméon Chardin painted quiet kitchens and children at play; Canaletto painted precise views of Venice for travelers on the Grand Tour.
topics.trouble: People think Canaletto's views are exact snapshots. He often adjusted buildings and viewpoints to fit the picture.

topics.title: The Grand Manner Portrait
topics.short: British portraitists such as Thomas Gainsborough (The Blue Boy, about 1770) and Joshua Reynolds posed sitters with dignity, rich fabric and landscape backgrounds.
topics.trouble: People think the portrait was a minor genre. Academies ranked it below history painting, but it paid most artists' bills.

topics.title: Neoclassicism
topics.short: After the digs at Pompeii, artists such as Jacques-Louis David turned to clear line, calm color and Roman virtue, as in The Oath of the Horatii (1784).
topics.trouble: People mix up Neoclassical and Renaissance art because both revive antiquity. Neoclassicism, about 1760 to 1830, is cooler and sharper and often carries a moral message.

topics.title: Art in Early America
topics.short: John Singleton Copley painted Paul Revere (1768) at his workbench; Gilbert Stuart painted George Washington; Jefferson designed Monticello on Roman and Palladian models.
topics.trouble: People think Revere's portrait shows a rider. Copley painted him as a silversmith holding a teapot he made, with his tools.

topics.title: Romanticism and the Sublime
topics.short: Romantic artists (about 1800 to 1850) valued feeling, nature's power and the individual: Caspar David Friedrich's Wanderer above the Sea of Fog and J. M. W. Turner's storms and sunsets.
topics.trouble: People think "romantic" means about love. Romanticism is about strong feeling, awe at nature (the sublime) and imagination.

topics.title: Constable and Goya
topics.short: John Constable painted the English countryside from close study, as in The Hay Wain (1821); Francisco Goya painted the Spanish court with sharp honesty.
topics.trouble: People think landscape painting was always respected. Academies ranked it low until painters like Constable and Turner raised it.

topics.title: The Hudson River School
topics.short: Thomas Cole, Frederic Church and Albert Bierstadt painted American wilderness on a grand scale; Cole's The Oxbow (1836) sets wild hills beside farmland.
topics.trouble: People think these painters copied one view exactly. They combined sketches from many places into ideal scenes.

topics.title: Realism
topics.short: Realists painted ordinary people and work without idealizing them: Courbet's Stone Breakers (1849), Millet's The Gleaners (1857) and Rosa Bonheur's The Horse Fair (1852–1855).
topics.trouble: People use "realism" to mean any lifelike picture. The 19th-century movement was about choosing everyday, unheroic subjects.

topics.title: Photography Arrives
topics.short: Louis Daguerre announced the daguerreotype in 1839; by the 1860s photographers such as Julia Margaret Cameron were making photographs as art.
topics.trouble: People think early photos needed only a click. Long exposures meant moving people vanished, which is why early street views look empty.

topics.title: American Painting after the Civil War
topics.short: Winslow Homer painted the sea and country life, John Singer Sargent dazzling portraits, and Henry Ossawa Tanner The Banjo Lesson (1893).
topics.trouble: People think American art only copied Europe. Homer, Eakins and Tanner trained partly abroad but painted distinctly American subjects.

topics.title: Ukiyo-e: Japanese Woodblock Prints
topics.short: Edo-period prints of the "floating world" were a team effort: a publisher, a designer such as Hokusai or Hiroshige, a carver and a printer, with one block for each color.
topics.trouble: People think Hokusai carved and printed The Great Wave himself. He designed it; carvers and printers made the blocks and prints.

topics.title: Japanese Screens and Castles
topics.short: Folding screens painted on gold leaf, such as Ogata Kōrin's Irises (about 1705), and castles like Himeji (completed 1609) show the splendor of Japan's great families.
topics.trouble: People read a folding screen as a flat painting. It stands in a zigzag, so the picture folds in and out with the light.

topics.title: Ming and Qing China
topics.short: The Ming built the Forbidden City in Beijing (1406–1420) and made fine blue-and-white porcelain; literati scholar-painters valued personal brushwork over likeness.
topics.trouble: People think "Ming vase" means any old Chinese vase. The Ming dynasty ruled from 1368 to 1644; the Qing came after.

topics.title: Joseon Korea
topics.short: Joseon Korea (1392–1897) prized plain white porcelain such as the round moon jars, and Jeong Seon painted "true-view" landscapes of real Korean mountains.
topics.trouble: People think Korean art is a branch of Chinese art. Korean painters and potters built their own styles and tastes.

topics.title: The Mughal Empire
topics.short: Mughal emperors in India sponsored jewel-like manuscript paintings and built the Taj Mahal (1632–1653), Shah Jahan's tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.
topics.trouble: People think the Taj Mahal is a palace. It is a tomb, set in a garden.

topics.title: Ottoman and Safavid Splendor
topics.short: The architect Sinan built the Süleymaniye Mosque in Istanbul (1550–1557) with Iznik tiles; in Isfahan the Safavid Shah Mosque (1611–about 1630) glows with blue tile.
topics.trouble: People think Ottoman mosques copied Hagia Sophia exactly. Sinan learned from it but built lighter domes with more windows.

topics.title: Impressionism
topics.short: The Impressionists painted light and modern life with visible broken brushstrokes, often outdoors; their first group show was in Paris in 1874, and Monet's Impression, Sunrise gave them their name.
topics.trouble: People think the Impressionists were sloppy. Their quick strokes were a careful method for catching changing light.

topics.title: Monet's Series
topics.short: Claude Monet painted the same subject, grainstacks, Rouen Cathedral, water lilies, again and again to show how light and weather change it.
topics.trouble: People think the series are copies of one picture. Each canvas records a different hour, season or weather.

topics.title: Degas, Renoir, Morisot and Cassatt
topics.short: Edgar Degas painted dancers and racehorses, Pierre-Auguste Renoir crowds at leisure, and Berthe Morisot and Mary Cassatt the lives of women and children.
topics.trouble: People think Degas painted outdoors like Monet. He worked mostly in the studio and disliked being called an Impressionist.

topics.title: Japonisme
topics.short: After Japan opened to trade in the 1850s, Japanese woodblock prints poured into Europe; their flat color, bold cropping and high viewpoints inspired Degas, Van Gogh and Cassatt.
topics.trouble: People think the influence went only one way. Japanese artists also adopted Western perspective and shading.

topics.title: Seurat and Pointillism
topics.short: Georges Seurat placed small dots of pure color side by side for the eye to blend, as in A Sunday on La Grande Jatte (1884–1886).
topics.trouble: People think the dots blend into smooth color up close. They blend only from a distance, and the effect shimmers rather than mixes like paint.

topics.title: Vincent van Gogh
topics.short: Van Gogh used thick paint (impasto), swirling strokes and strong color to express feeling, as in The Starry Night (1889) and his Sunflowers (1888).
topics.trouble: People think Van Gogh painted only a few pictures. He made more than 850 paintings in about ten years.

topics.title: Cézanne and Gauguin
topics.short: Paul Cézanne built landscapes and still lifes from patches of color and simple forms, a path toward Cubism; Paul Gauguin used flat, bold color and outlines.
topics.trouble: People think Cézanne's tilted tables are mistakes. He combined several viewpoints on purpose.

topics.title: Masks, Figures and Textiles in Africa
topics.short: Many African masks and figures were made for performance and ceremony, seen in motion with costume, music and dance; textiles such as Asante kente carry meaning in their patterns.
topics.trouble: People judge a mask as a still object on a museum wall. Most were meant to be worn and danced, with a full costume.

topics.title: The Benin Bronzes
topics.short: Guilds in the Kingdom of Benin (in today's Nigeria) cast brass plaques and heads for the Oba's palace from the 1500s on; British troops took thousands of them in 1897.
topics.trouble: People think the Benin Bronzes come from the modern Republic of Benin, or that they are all bronze. They come from the old Kingdom of Benin, in today's Nigeria, and most are brass.

topics.title: Arts of Native North America
topics.short: Northwest Coast carvers made totem poles in formline style; Navajo weavers made striped blankets; Plains artists drew on ledger paper; Pueblo potters made painted and polished pottery.
topics.trouble: People speak of "Native American art" as one style. Hundreds of nations made very different arts, and many still do.

topics.title: Fauvism and Expressionism
topics.short: Around 1905 the Fauves, led by Henri Matisse, used wild, unnatural color; German Expressionists such as Ernst Ludwig Kirchner and Franz Marc used color and distortion to express feeling.
topics.trouble: People think the Fauves couldn't see real colors. They chose color for feeling and design, not description.

topics.title: Cubism
topics.short: Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque, from about 1907, broke objects into facets seen from several viewpoints at once; Juan Gris and others carried it on.
topics.trouble: People think Cubism is about cubes. The name came from a critic's remark; the idea is many viewpoints in one picture.

topics.title: The First Abstract Paintings
topics.short: Between about 1910 and 1915, Wassily Kandinsky, Kazimir Malevich and others made paintings that show no objects at all, only color, line and shape.
topics.trouble: People think abstract art is random. Its makers planned color, balance and rhythm, and often wrote long explanations of their aims.

topics.title: Futurism and Dada
topics.short: Italian Futurists (from 1909) glorified speed and machines; Dada artists in Zurich (from 1916) and beyond mocked art itself, as in Marcel Duchamp's Fountain (1917).
topics.trouble: People think Dada was meant to be beautiful. It was a protest against war and against the art world's rules.

topics.title: De Stijl and the Bauhaus
topics.short: Piet Mondrian reduced painting to black lines and primary colors; the Bauhaus school in Germany (1919–1933) joined art, craft and industry in modern design.
topics.trouble: People think Mondrian's grids were quick to make. He adjusted line widths and spacing for weeks to get the balance right.

topics.title: Surrealism
topics.short: Surrealists, after André Breton's manifesto of 1924, painted dreams and the unconscious: Salvador Dalí's melting watches and René Magritte's puzzles.
topics.trouble: People call any odd picture surreal. The movement aimed to free the unconscious mind, often with very precise painting.

topics.title: Modern Architecture
topics.short: Louis Sullivan's skyscrapers ("form follows function"), Frank Lloyd Wright's Robie House (1910) and Fallingwater (1935–1939), and Art Deco towers like the Chrysler Building (1930).
topics.trouble: People think a skyscraper's walls hold it up. A steel frame carries the weight; the outer walls hang on it.

topics.title: American Modernism
topics.short: Georgia O'Keeffe painted close-up flowers and desert forms; Edward Hopper lonely city scenes; Harlem Renaissance artists such as Aaron Douglas and, later, Jacob Lawrence told Black American history.
topics.trouble: People think American art followed Europe until the 1940s. O'Keeffe, Hopper and the Harlem Renaissance built American modern art before then.

topics.title: Mexican Muralism and Frida Kahlo
topics.short: After the Mexican Revolution, Diego Rivera, José Clemente Orozco and David Alfaro Siqueiros painted public murals of Mexican history; Frida Kahlo painted personal self-portraits.
topics.trouble: People think Frida Kahlo was a muralist. She painted mostly small self-portraits; her husband Diego Rivera painted the murals.

topics.title: Photography as Modern Art
topics.short: Alfred Stieglitz fought for photography as art (The Steerage, 1907); Dorothea Lange's Migrant Mother (1936) made the Great Depression visible.
topics.trouble: People think a documentary photo is unposed and unchosen. Photographers choose the moment, the frame and which print to show.

topics.title: Abstract Expressionism
topics.short: In New York after World War II, Jackson Pollock dripped paint on canvas laid on the floor, and Mark Rothko painted glowing fields of color.
topics.trouble: People say "my kid could do that." Pollock's pours were controlled and practiced, and Rothko built color in many thin layers.

topics.title: Telling the Styles Apart
topics.short: Each period has telltale signs: Gothic pointed arches, Renaissance balance, Baroque drama, Rococo pastels, Neoclassical clarity, Impressionist strokes, Cubist facets.
topics.trouble: People recognize styles by famous names only. Look for the visual clues, and a new work becomes readable.

topics.title: Dating a Work by Its Style
topics.short: Clothes, subject, technique, materials and style narrow a work's date before any document is found.
topics.trouble: People rely on one clue. Several clues together give a safer date.

topics.title: Comparing Two Works
topics.short: Comparing two works side by side, subject, composition, color, technique and purpose, shows what is special about each.
topics.trouble: People describe one work and then the other. A good comparison sets them against each other point by point.
